title: Two weeks thirsty
objective: Tell DKA from HHS: DKA is acute with low mortality, while HHS develops over weeks and has a much higher mortality rate

brief.situation: 16:00 on a medical unit. You are the RN admitting Mr. Ortiz, 79, from an assisted living home. He has type 2 diabetes on oral medication and heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction. Staff say he has been 'drinking water all day and peeing constantly' for about two weeks and became confused yesterday.
handover: Emergency department labs: glucose 890 mg/dL, sodium 134, potassium pending, bicarbonate 22, pH 7.36, beta-hydroxybutyrate 0.6 mmol/L, calculated effective osmolality 340.
The admitting order set reads: isotonic fluid as ordered, then an insulin infusion per the hyperglycemic crisis protocol. The protocol says insulin is not started until potassium is above 3.5 mmol/L.
He has had no fluid yet. The hospitalist is on the unit.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

why.question: Is this DKA or HHS, and what do you do first?

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: HHS: glucose over 600, effective osmolality over 300, little ketosis and no acidosis; it develops over days to weeks, mostly in older adults with type 2 diabetes, and has a much higher mortality than DKA, which is acute.
parts.modelAnswer: This is HHS, not DKA: sugar 890, osmolality 340, barely any ketones and a normal pH. It crept up over two weeks, and it's the more deadly of the two, especially at 79.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Starts the ordered isotonic fluid with close lung checks given heart failure, holds insulin until potassium is above 3.5, checks the rhythm and neuro status, and calls the provider for potassium replacement.
parts.modelAnswer: Fluids first at the ordered rate, listening to his lungs because of his heart failure, hold the insulin because his potassium is 3.1, check the monitor and his neuro status, and call the hospitalist for potassium.

arrhythmia.headline: Hypokalemic dysrhythmia
arrhythmia.body: HHS: fluids first, and check potassium before insulin. Insulin with a potassium of 3.1 drives it lower and can cause a fatal rhythm.

safe.headline: HHS treated in order
safe.body: You told HHS from DKA, started fluid at the ordered rate with his heart in mind, held insulin for a low potassium and called within minutes. That is the expert path.

safeGaps.body: Check how soon you called, whether insulin started with low potassium, and whether fluid ran wide open in heart failure.

scoring.modelReasoning: HHS is a glucose of 600 mg/dL or more with an effective osmolality over 300 and little ketosis or acidosis; it develops over days to weeks, usually in older adults with type 2 diabetes, and has a much higher mortality than DKA, which comes on acutely. Treatment starts with isotonic fluid (smaller boluses in older adults and heart failure), then insulin, with potassium measured first: if it is low, insulin is postponed until potassium is above 3.5 mmol/L, because insulin drives potassium into cells. Osmolality should fall slowly.

kQ.ask: While he transfers: why wait on insulin?

choices.label: Insulin moves potassium into cells; with potassium under 3.5 it is postponed

kQ.explain: If potassium is low at presentation, insulin is postponed until potassium is above 3.5 mmol/L.
